name: LOW World Championship
epitaph: Lights Out Wrestling's own top prize, and the belt its whole first year of storyline ran through: CADE was billed as the first man to hold it, Mike Meyhu took it and the presidency together after turning on Trigger, and Tristan Belmont, Jason Ortiz, Jason Kage and Donny Diamond carried it across the fed's second run. Annihilation won it in an Asylum Match at CATASTROPHIC in October 2004 and hanged himself on the wire that lowered it to him in the same segment; the fed's own masthead banner shows the belt vacant six weeks later. No title ledger of LOW's own survives; what is known of the lineage comes from the fed's own bio cards, its served shows and the champion banner it stamped into the masthead of every page.

name: LOW Xtreme Championship
epitaph: The belt that carried the fed's own tagline — Lights Out Wrestling billed itself "Xtreme Has Returned" and named a championship after the word. Annihilation, Reality/Mayhem, Iron Lung, Angelus Sorrow, Psymon, Juvian Ramorez, Dark Haze and Eric Russo all held it across three years. Iron Lung defended it on Realm 48 in a thirty-count Warrior Match and lost it three weeks later to Angelus Sorrow in an Ultimate Taipei Match with broken glass glued to the ropes; Ramorez took it off Psymon at CATASTROPHIC in a two-out-of-three-falls match the fed's own commentary called stolen.

name: LOW Realm Championship
epitaph: Named for Realm, the weekly show it was defended on, this was Lights Out Wrestling's own mid-card championship and the one its record tracks most closely: Eric Russo, Jason Ortiz, Cyrus Skar, Malik Katsuya, The Demond, Ron Diamond and Brody Dahmer all held it. Cyrus Skar's own bio card records him as Realm Champion "until LOW closed for the 1st time" — the belt outlasting the fed's own first run — and he lost it on the fiftieth Realm without being pinned, stripped mid-match by the fed's own president for attacking his valet.

name: LOW Aftermath Championship
epitaph: The championship of Aftermath, the midweek show Lights Out Wrestling ran alongside Realm. Iron Lung, Pax, Jason Warrior, Tyrone Johnson and Kimi Aikohana are the champions the fed's own record names; Jason Warrior's own bio card dates his reign precisely, from the In The End pay-per-view of 11 June 2003 to Wakeup Call on 31 August 2003, and says he relinquished it rather than lost it. Pax's own bio card lists "LOW Aftermath Champ[Creator]" among the LOW titles it gives, a claim to the belt's creation, and Iron Lung's own manager came back at Shellshock for a belt he said he had won himself.

name: LOW Tag Team Championship
epitaph: Lights Out Wrestling's own tag team championship, held for long stretches by one pairing under two names: Eric Russo and Jason Kage won it in August 2002 and held it again from August 2003 as the Metallo Zords, and The Gold Ranger and The Silver Ranger — the Zords' own two members, named as such on the team's own bio card — record the same reigns on their own cards. The Saikyo System took the belts off them up a ladder on the fiftieth Realm, and Delta Upsilon Iota, a fraternity act of Colby Korver and Hank Cobb, held them through CATASTROPHIC.
notes: SOURCES DISAGREE on who the Metallo Zords were. Jason Kage's and Eric Russo's own bio cards each record a Tag Team Championship reign "as the Metallo Zords" from 18 August 2003; The Gold Ranger's and The Silver Ranger's own cards record a Tag Team Championship reign of their own across the same period. Both readings are recorded rather than resolved. The team's own bio card settles who the Metallo Zords were even where it does not settle whose reign this was: its kayfabe Real Name field reads "Gold Ranger and Silver Ranger".

name: LOW King of the Death Match
epitaph: An annual crown rather than a defended belt, and the one honour Lights Out Wrestling carried in its masthead banner alongside its five championships. Adam Stryker is recorded as the 2004 King of the Death Match and Donny Diamond as the 2005; no other year survives in the fed's own record.
notes: Won once a year in the fed's own tournament — a bracket entered by invitation, run over rounds with byes and a final, and settled on the night — and never defended between crownings. Its own masthead banner carried the reigning king in the same strip of champion portraits as its five championships, and one of its own bio cards lists the crown among a wrestler's LOW titles. No defence of it survives anywhere in the fed's own record.
